paragraphs: Maria L. Okafor, David Chen, Priya Raman

sections.heading: Abstract
paragraphs: We examined whether extended sleep improves working-memory performance. In a randomized controlled trial (n = 96), participants who slept nine hours outperformed a control group (p < 0.001, 95% CI: 2.1 to 4.8). Prior work has been mixed (Kim, 2018; Alvarez & Novak, 2021).

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Working memory is central to reasoning. Earlier studies suggested a link between sleep and cognition, but effect sizes varied widely. Okafor et al. (2019) reported a moderate effect, whereas Delgado (2017) found none.

sections.heading: Methods
paragraphs: Ninety-six healthy adults were randomized into two groups (n = 96). We used an independent t-test to compare group means and a one-way ANOVA to assess dose response across three sleep durations. Categorical outcomes were analyzed with a chi-square test.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs: Table 1 reports the primary outcomes. The extended-sleep group scored higher on the n-back task (p < 0.001, 95% CI: 2.1 to 4.8). A secondary analysis showed a dose effect (p = 0.02). These findings replicate Okafor et al. (2019).

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Our results support a causal role for sleep in working memory. The effect was robust across analyses, consistent with earlier reports (Alvarez & Novak, 2021).

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Extended sleep improves working memory in healthy adults.
